quotes.t: Would you not think him an utter fool who wept because he was not alive a thousand years ago? And is he not just as much of a fool who weeps because he will not be alive a thousand years from now? It is all the same; you will not be, and you were not. Neither of these periods of time belongs to you.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LXXVII: On Taking One's Own Life

quotes.t: Would you really know what philosophy offers to humanity? Philosophy offers counsel.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.t: You do not know where death awaits you; so be ready for it everywhere.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XXVI: On Old Age and Death

quotes.t: You have demanded of me, Novatus, that I should write how anger may be soothed, and it appears to me that you are right in feeling especial fear of this passion, which is above all others hideous and wild: for the others have some alloy of peace and quiet, but this consists wholly in action and the impulse of grief, raging with an utterly inhuman lust for arms, blood and tortures, careless of itself provided it hurts another, rushing upon the very point of the sword, and greedy for revenge even when it drags the avenger to ruin with itself.
quotes.c: Dialogues, On Anger to Novatus

quotes.t: You have, dearest Serene, things that can protect tranquility, things that restore it, things that resist creeping escapes. Be it known, however, that none of these things is sufficient for those who hold a feeble matter, unless a constant concern surrounds the slipping mind.
quotes.c: Dialogues, Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

quotes.t: You must die erect and unyielding.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XXXVII: On Allegiance to Virtue

quotes.t: You must go now, fellow-soldiers, to yonder place, whence there is no 'must' about your returning!
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LXXXII: On the Natural Fear of Death, Seneca is citing Marcus Calpurnius Flamma, a Roman general in the First Punic War

quotes.t: You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

quotes.t: You need a change of soul rather than a change of climate.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

quotes.t: You will die, not because you are ill, but because you are alive; even when you have been cured, thesame end awaits you; when you have recovered, it will be not death, but ill health, that you have escaped.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.t: You will thus understand that what you fear is either insignificant or short-lived.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.t: arma non servant modum; nec temperari facile nec reprimi potest stricti ensis ira; bella delectat cruor.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), Arms observe no bounds; nor can the wrath of the sword, once drawn, be easily checked or stayed; war delights in blood. lines 403-405; (Lycus).

quotes.t: ars prima regni est posse invidiam pati.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), 'Tis the first art of kings, the power to suffer hate. line 353; (Lycus) Alternate translation: To be able to endure odium is the first art to be learned by those who aspire to power (translator unknown).

quotes.t: bonus iudex damnat inprobanda, non odit.
quotes.c: Moral Essays, A good judge condemns wrongful acts, but does not hate them. De Ira (On Anger): Book 1, cap. 16, line 6.

quotes.t: errant consilia nostra, quia non habent quo derigantur; ignoranti quem portum petat nullus suus ventus est.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LXXI: On the supreme good, Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind. Line 2 Alternate translation: If one does not know to which port one is sailing, no wind is favorable. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: fidei acerrimus exactor est perfidus
quotes.c: Moral Essays, No man expects such exact fidelity as a traitor. De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 28, line 7.

quotes.t: inveniet viam aut faciet.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), He will find a way - or make one. line 276; (Amphitryon) In this line, Seneca adapts a well-known saying "Inveniam viam aut faciam" (commonly attributed to the Carthaginian general Hannibal) for use in his drama

quotes.t: mens regnum bona possidet.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Thyestes, Tis the upright mind that holds true sovereignty. line 380; (Chorus) Alternate translation: A good mind possesses a kingdom. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: might have accomplished something more successful in that camp, but never anything more brave.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.t: nemo autem regere potest nisi qui et regi.
quotes.c: Moral Essays, No one is able to rule unless he is also able to be ruled. De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 15, line 4 Compare with the following: No man ruleth safely but that he is willingly ruled. From The Imitation of Christ, Liber I, cap. 20 (Of the Love of Solitude and Silence), line 2: by Thomas à Kempis (1380-1471).

quotes.t: numquam vacat lascivire districtis, nihilque tam certum est quam otii vitia negotio discuti.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LVI: On quiet and study, The much occupied man has no time for wantonness, and it is an obvious commonplace that the evils of leisure can be shaken off by hard work. Line 9 Alternate translation: Nothing is so certain as that the evils of idleness can be shaken off by hard work. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: peior est bello timor ipse belli.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Thyestes, Worse than war is the very fear of war. line 572 (Chorus).

quotes.t: postea noli rogare quod inpetrare nolueris.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XCV: On the usefulness of basic principles, Don't ask for what you'll wish you hadn't got. Line 1 Seneca himself states that he is quoting a 'common saying' here. Alternate translation: Do not ask for what you will wish you had not got. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: quae fuit durum pati, meminisse dulce est.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), Things 'twas hard to bear 'tis pleasant to recall. lines 656-657; (Amphitryon) Alternate translation: Things that were hard to bear are sweet to remember. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: quaeritur belli exitus, non causa.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), Of war men ask the outcome, not the cause. line 407; (Lycus).

quotes.t: qualis quisque sit scies, si quemadmodum laudet, quemadmodum laudetur aspexeris.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LII: On choosing our teachers, You can tell the character of every man when you see how he gives and receives praise. Line 12.

quotes.t: quemadmodum gladius neminem occidit: occidentis telum est.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter LXXXVII: Some arguments in favor of the simple life, A sword by itself does not slay; it is merely the weapon used by the slayer. Line 30 Seneca is here describing arguments used by 'certain men,' not stating his own opinion. Alternate translation: A sword never kills anybody; it is a tool in the killer's hand. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: qui genus iactat suum, aliena laudat.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), Who vaunts his race, lauds what belongs to others. lines 340-341; (Lycus). Alternate translation: He who boasts of his descent, praises the deeds of another (translator unknown).

quotes.t: quid est sapienta? semper idem velle atque idem nolle.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XX: On practicing what you preach, What is wisdom? Always desiring the same things, and always refusing the same things. Line 5 Here, Seneca uses the same observation that Sallust made regarding friendship (in his historical account of the Catilinarian conspiracy, Bellum Catilinae) to define wisdom.

quotes.t: rursus prosperum ac felix scelus virtus vocatur; sontibus parent boni, ius est in armis, opprimit leges timor.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules), Once again prosperous and successful crime goes by the name of virtue; good men obey the bad, might is right and fear oppresses law. lines 251-253; (Amphitryon) Alternate translation: Successful and fortunate crime is called virtue. (translator unknown) Alternate translation: Might makes right. (translator unknown).

quotes.t: scelere velandum est scelus.
quotes.c: Tragedies, Phaedra, Sin must be hid by sin. line 721; (Nurse) Alternate translation: One crime has to be concealed by another.

quotes.t: sciant quae optima sunt esse communia.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XII: On old age, The best ideas are common property. Line 11.

quotes.t: sic cum inferiore vivas quemadmodum tecum superiorem velis vivere.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter XLVII: On master and slave, Treat your inferiors as you would be treated by your betters. Line 11 This can be related to other expressions on the ethics of reciprocity, often referred to as the variants of the Golden Rule.

quotes.t: sic vive cum hominibus tamquam deus videat, si loquere cum deo tamquam homines audiant.
quotes.c: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter X: On living to oneself, Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening. Line 5.

quotes.t: No man was ever wise by chance.
Most powerful is he who has himself in his own power.
The greatest remedy for anger is delay.
As long as you live, keep learning how to live.
Consult your friend on all things, especially on those which respect yourself. His counsel may then be useful where your own self-love might impair your judgment.
Difficulties strengthen the mind, as labor does the body.
Friendship always benefits; love sometimes injures.
If a man knows not to which port he sails, no wind is favorable.
If one does not know to which port is sailing, no wind is favorable.
If one does not know to which port one is sailing, no wind is favorable.
It is another's fault if he be ungrateful, but it is mine if I do not give. To find one thankful man, I will oblige a great many that are not so.
One of the most beautiful qualities of true friendship is to understand and to be understood.
The conditions of conquest are always easy. We have but to toil awhile, endure awhile, believe always, and never turn back.
The mind unlearns with difficulty what it has long learned.
There is no great genius without some touch of madness.
Things that were hard to bear are sweet to remember.
We are more often frightened than hurt; and we suffer more from imagination than from reality.
A sword never kills anybody; it is a tool in the killer's hand.
Associate with people who are likely to improve your own character and not harm it.
Associate with people who will make you better, not those who will make you popular.
Call it Nature, Fate, Fortune all these are names of the one and selfsame God.
He who fears death will never do anything worth of a man who lives forever.

I never come back home with the same moral character I went out with something or other becomes unsettled where I had achieved internal peace some one or other of the things I had put to flight reappears on the scene.
I shall never be ashamed of citing a bad author if the line is good.
If you wish to improve, be content to appear clueless or stupid in extraneous matters.
If you wish to improve, be content to appear clunsy and awkward.
It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.
It is not that we have little time, but that we waste much of it.
It is the characteristic of the wise to resist pleasures and to be the masters of them, not slaves.
It is the nature of the wise to resist piercings by the thorns of fortune.
It is the nature of the wise to resist pleasures, but the foolish to be a slave to them.
It is the quality of our work which will please and live, not the quantity.
Life is long if you know how to use it.
No man has been found so wise as to prefer evil to good, yet nearly all men are not wise enough to prefer a greater good to a less.
No man has had a happy life that he thoroughly repented of.
No man has had enough time, if you consider what he has wasted.
No man is more unhappy than he who cannot cast off his past.
No man is more unhappy than he who never faces adversity. For he is never permitted to prove himself.
The condition upon which God hath given liberty to man is eternal vigilance.
The greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which depends on tomorrow and loses today.
There is none made so great, but he may both need the help and service, and stand in fear of the power and unkindness, even of the meanest of mortals.
We should every night call our souls to an account.

We should every night call to mind how we have acted that day, and how we have spent it; what vices we have overcome, what we have been overcome by; in what respects we have been lazy, in what indulgent.
We should every night call to mind what we have done wrong, what we have done right, and what we ought to do better.
